nameStory: This microscopic green alga gets its scientific name from Brazil, where it was first discovered and described by scientists. The genus name Desmodesmus means 'bound together' in Greek, referring to how these tiny cells link up in chains or colonies that you can sometimes see floating in still water.
description: **Note: This identification is uncertain as this appears to be a microscopic freshwater alga, not a typical plant covered by this guide.** Desmodesmus brasiliensis is a single-celled green alga that forms small colonies in freshwater. Individual cells are incredibly tiny - far too small to see without a microscope - but sometimes their colonies create faint greenish films or clouds in still water. This is definitely a species that requires laboratory equipment to properly identify.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual cells are invisible to the naked eye - you'll need a microscope to see the characteristic oval-shaped cells arranged in groups of 2, 4, or 8

idTips.label: Colony formation
idTips.description: Cells stick together in small clusters that may create barely visible green specks floating in water

idTips.label: Freshwater habitat
idTips.description: Found only in fresh water - never in salt water or on land surfaces

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: When present in large numbers, may tint water with a faint greenish color that has no particular smell

habitat: Found in quiet freshwater environments like ponds, slow streams, and temporary pools throughout New England's lower elevations. Prefers nutrient-rich water and may be more common in areas with some organic matter or gentle water movement.

seasonality.spring: Most active during warming weather when water temperatures rise and daylight increases, potentially creating faint green tints in still water.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when colonies may be most visible as greenish films in warm, sunny ponds and slow waterways.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases as temperatures drop and daylight shortens, becoming much less noticeable in cooling waters.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant in cold water, essentially invisible and inactive until spring warming begins.

funFact: Despite being impossibly tiny, these single-celled organisms can actually 'communicate' with each other through chemical signals to coordinate when to reproduce - like a microscopic social network happening right under our noses in every pond!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other microscopic green algae that create similar faint green films in water. Without a microscope and expertise in algae identification, it's nearly impossible to distinguish from dozens of other single-celled green algae species.
contextualKnowledge: This species highlights how much hidden microscopic life exists in every drop of pond water - what looks like empty water to us is actually teeming with countless tiny organisms. Most nature guides focus on plants and animals we can easily see, but algae like this form the foundation of aquatic food webs.
compareHints: **Identification uncertain** - Distinguishing this species from other Desmodesmus species requires detailed microscopic examination of cell shape, colony arrangement, and reproductive structures. Other species in this genus may form different colony patterns or have slightly different cell shapes, but these differences are only visible under laboratory conditions with proper magnification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives like Desmodesmus communis, this species lacks the prominent spines or teeth on the outer cells that characterize many other Desmodesmus species.
